title: Class Delivery – Learner Commands
overview:
Class Delivery – Learner Commands

Nov 15, 2026 · @Someone

This handout holds every command and prompt we run in the live class, with the result you should see after each one. Each tab matches one part of the session.

How to use this handout

  • Run in Terminal blocks are shell commands. The setup follows macOS.

  • Paste into Codex blocks are prompts. Send them exactly as written unless the step says to replace a value.

  • Expected lines describe what a correct result looks like. Exact wording, file names and amounts from Codex can differ.

  • Each tab ends with a checkpoint. Confirm every item before moving to the next tab.

  • Keep Codex on Medium reasoning throughout unless a step says otherwise.

Open a tab

Each part of the class is its own tab. Use the Tabs menu in the bar at the top of this doc, or click a tab below.

tabs.name: 01 Setup
tabs.html:
Tab 01 — Introduction and One-Time Setup

Goal: Install and verify the tools, download the reference project, and prepare the workshop. We won't build or run the auction app in this tab.

1. Tools we use

Tool

Its role

Codex

Helps us plan, write, test, and review code

Git

Downloads the repository and tracks changes

Node.js

Runs JavaScript applications and development tools

npm

Installs the project's dependencies

Docker Desktop

Runs supporting services such as PostgreSQL

VS Code

Lets us inspect code and project instructions

Microsoft Edge

Runs the prepared browser tests later in the course

These instructions follow the macOS setup.

2. Check the tools

Run in Terminal — any folder:

git --version
node --version
npm --version
docker --version
code --version

Expected: each command prints its installed version. If you see command not found, install that tool or fix its command-line setup. Use Node.js 22 LTS, version 22.12 or newer.

Install missing tools:

Tool

Installation

Node.js

https://nodejs.org/en/download

Docker Desktop

https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/

VS Code

https://code.visualstudio.com/

Microsoft Edge

https://www.microsoft.com/edge

Codex

https://developers.openai.com/codex/

If Git is missing:

xcode-select --install

If VS Code opens but code is unavailable:

  1. Open VS Code.

  2. Press Cmd+Shift+P.

  3. Select Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH.

  4. Reopen Terminal.

Open Edge once and complete its first-run setup.

3. Optional: Homebrew installation

Only use this route if Homebrew is installed:

brew --version

Install missing command-line tools:

brew install node@22 git gh python

Use Node 22 in the current terminal:

export PATH="$(brew --prefix node@22)/bin:$PATH"

To make this the default, append the setting once:

echo 'export PATH="$(brew --prefix node@22)/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc

Install missing applications:

brew install --cask docker microsoft-edge visual-studio-code

Checkpoint: All five version commands work, and Edge opens.

4. Verify Docker's engine

Open Docker Desktop, complete any initial setup, and wait for its engine to start.

Run in Terminal:

docker info --format 'Docker is running: {{.ServerVersion}}'

Expected:

Docker is running: <version>

Also check Compose:

docker compose version

Expected: a Docker Compose version number. If you see "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon", wait for Docker Desktop to finish starting and retry.

5. Download the completed reference

Run in Terminal:

mkdir -p ~/codex-course
cd ~/codex-course
ls

If reference or workshop already exists, inspect it before continuing. The clone commands below expect those destination folders not to exist.

git clone https://github.com/schneidenbach/master-dot-dev-codex-course-live.git reference
ls reference

Expected: the eight part-... folders and shared files such as:

AGENTS.md
README.md
docker-compose.yml
scripts
stripe-service

6. Prepare the workshop

Run in Terminal:

cd ~/codex-course
git clone https://github.com/schneidenbach/master-dot-dev-codex-course-live.git workshop

The next block deletes the downloaded contents of Parts 2–8 in this new workshop copy, recreates those directories empty, and starts a fresh Git history.

(
  cd ~/codex-course/workshop || exit 1
  for d in part-[2-8]-*; do
    [ -d "$d" ] || continue
    rm -rf -- "$d"
    mkdir -- "$d"
  done
  rm -rf .git
  git init -q
  git add -A
  git commit -m "Workshop start: part 1 only"
)

If the commit fails because Git needs your identity, set it for this workshop:

git -C ~/codex-course/workshop config user.name "Your Name"
git -C ~/codex-course/workshop config user.email "your-email@example.com"

Then retry:

git -C ~/codex-course/workshop commit -m "Workshop start: part 1 only"

7. Verify the starting point

Run in Terminal:

ls ~/codex-course/workshop/part-1-foundation

Expected: files and folders including package.json, server, and web.

Check that Parts 2–8 are empty:

(
  cd ~/codex-course/workshop || exit 1
  for d in part-[2-8]-*; do
    printf '%s: ' "$d"
    ls -A "$d" | wc -l
  done
)

Expected: each folder reports 0.

Check the saved starting point:

git -C ~/codex-course/workshop status

Expected:

nothing to commit, working tree clean

Your structure is now:

~/codex-course/
├── reference/              Completed application; comparison copy
└── workshop/               Our working copy
    ├── part-1-foundation/  Supplied starter code
    ├── part-2-.../         Empty
    ├── ...
    └── part-8-.../         Empty

8. Prepare Codex

Open Codex and verify that you can sign in.

The course settings are GPT-5.6 Sol, Medium reasoning, and "Approve for me". If your app offers different models or labels, use an available capable coding model with Medium reasoning and the corresponding routine-action approval setting.

The original course uses an OpenAI API-key sign-in. API usage is billed separately from a ChatGPT subscription. With a ChatGPT sign-in, some features and screens may differ.

No project-building prompt is needed here.

Completion checkpoint

  • Tools are installed and version checks pass.

  • Docker's engine and Compose work.

  • reference contains all eight completed parts.

  • workshop contains Part 1, with Parts 2–8 empty.

  • The workshop's starting commit exists.

  • Codex opens and you can sign in.

tabs.name: 02 Understanding Codex
tabs.html:
Tab 02 — Understanding Codex

Outcome: You can use Codex's chat, find its settings, and open its terminal. No project coding yet.

The Codex window

Area

What it holds

Sidebar

Projects and conversations

Chat

Instructions, responses, and action results

Terminal

Commands and application servers

Changes / review view

Edited files to inspect, when available

A project is our working folder. A chat is a conversation about a task.

Demonstration 1 — Send a message

Type into Codex:

hello world

Expected: Codex replies. Enter sends a message and Shift+Enter inserts a new line.

Demonstration 2 — Find the working settings

Setting

What it means

Model

Which AI model performs the task

Reasoning effort

How much reasoning it spends; use Medium for now

Approvals

Which actions can proceed automatically and which require review

The course uses GPT-5.6 Sol, Medium, Standard speed, and Approve for me. Use the available equivalents if your app's options differ.

If available, set Settings → General → Default file open destination → VS Code.

Demonstration 3 — Open the terminal

Run in Codex's terminal, or the Mac Terminal app:

pwd

Expected: the path of your current folder. Always check the terminal is in the right project before installing dependencies or changing files.

Completion checkpoint

  • You sent a message.

  • You located the model and approval settings.

  • You ran pwd.

tabs.name: 03 Reasoning Effort
tabs.html:
Tab 03 — Choosing Reasoning Effort and Managing Usage

Outcome: You understand when to increase reasoning effort and how to monitor usage. No coding in this tab.

Match effort to the task

Task

Starting point

Simple explanation or small, clear change

Lower effort

Normal development work

Medium

Difficult debugging or complex design decisions

Higher effort

For this course, stay on Medium. Effort labels and available levels may differ between app versions.

Demonstration 1 — Locate the effort setting

Open the model menu and find Effort or Reasoning. Leave Medium selected.

Demonstration 2 — Reusable instructions

Open Settings → Personalization → Custom instructions, if available. Custom instructions hold preferences that apply across conversations. Later, we use AGENTS.md for instructions specific to our project.

Don't save any instruction now.

Demonstration 3 — Usage and spending controls

For an API-key sign-in, open:

https://platform.openai.com/usage

Then open the billing and limits settings:

https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/limits

Expected: your usage so far and the spending notifications available to your account. A monthly budget is not a guaranteed hard stop; some budget settings only send alerts. Read the current setting's description.

For a ChatGPT sign-in, use the usage information available in the app instead.

Completion checkpoint

  • You can explain why renaming a variable and investigating a difficult concurrency bug need different reasoning effort.

  • Medium is still selected.

tabs.name: 04 Tech Stack
tabs.html:
Tab 04 — Understanding the Project and Tech Stack

Outcome: You understand the application's main components and repository structure. No coding yet.

The basic flow

Browser interface → Backend API → PostgreSQL

The frontend displays the interface, the backend processes requests and enforces rules, and the database stores information.

Demonstration 1 — Explore the reference project

Run in Terminal:

code ~/codex-course/reference

Expected: VS Code opens the reference project. Open README.md and find its stack description and part folders.

Technology

Its job in our project

TypeScript

Adds type checking to our JavaScript code

React + Vite

Builds and serves the browser interface

Fastify

Handles backend API requests

Zod

Validates incoming data

PostgreSQL

Stores users, auctions, and bids

Socket.IO + Redis

Delivers live updates across connected browsers and server instances

RabbitMQ

Carries messages between background processes

OpenTelemetry + Jaeger

Records and displays traces across services

Playwright

Tests application behavior in a real browser

Docker Compose

Runs supporting services in containers

Demonstration 2 — The project's organization

Open part-1-foundation:

File or folder

Purpose

web/

Frontend code

server/

Backend code

package.json

Dependencies and runnable scripts

AGENTS.md

Instructions for the coding agent

GRILL.md

Design questions and agreed decisions

CODEX.md

Record of prompts and development work

Then open the root docker-compose.yml.

Optional — run in Terminal:

cd ~/codex-course/workshop
docker compose config --services

Expected: a list of the configured services. This does not start them.

Demonstration 3 — Reference versus workshop

Run in Terminal:

ls ~/codex-course/workshop/part-1-foundation
ls -A ~/codex-course/workshop/part-2-create-auction-and-bid

Expected: Part 1 lists its files. Part 2 prints nothing because it is empty.

Completion checkpoint

  • You can name the job of the frontend, the backend and the database.

  • You can say where the rule "a seller cannot bid on their own auction" must be enforced: the backend. The frontend can also prevent it for usability.

tabs.name: 05 First Build & Skills
tabs.html:
Tab 05 — First AI Build and Custom Skills

Outcome: Generate a practice auction website, install the course skills, and review the result.

This is a disposable practice site. It won't become our workshop application.

1. Create the practice project

Run in Terminal:

mkdir -p ~/codex-course/auctionhouse-throwaway

In Codex, add or select this folder as your project:

~/codex-course/auctionhouse-throwaway

Start a new chat. Keep reasoning on Medium.

2. Send the first build prompt

Paste into Codex:

I would like to build an auction site. It's going to roughly
model how other popular auction sites look online.

Please use React.

Keep it to two routes right now:
- Home page with auctions on it and six sample auctions.
- A separate route to view an individual auction.

Build it with three different looks/themes. Make them available
on the homepage and let me click between them.

Expected: Codex creates a React project with a homepage, an auction detail route and a theme switcher, then reports a completion summary.

3. Install the course skills while Codex builds

Use a separate Terminal window so you don't interrupt the build.

Run in Terminal:

npx skills@latest add schneidenbach/skills

Follow the installer prompts and select:

domain-modeling
grill-me
grill-with-docs
grilling

Choose installation for Codex, with global scope. Installer wording may vary; complete all prompts and wait for the success summary. Preserve any unrelated skills already installed.

Verify:

ls ~/.agents/skills

Expected: the four skill folders are listed.

Open one skill:

code ~/.agents/skills/grilling/SKILL.md

Expected: a readable SKILL.md file of instructions opens in VS Code.

4. Check that Codex can discover the skills

After the build finishes, type this into Codex without sending it:

/grill

Expected: the installed grilling skills appear in the menu. Clear the text afterward. If they don't appear, confirm installation finished and restart Codex if necessary.

5. Review and run the generated website

Read Codex's completion summary and open its changed-files or review view.

In Codex's project terminal, confirm your location:

pwd

Expected: a path ending with:

/codex-course/auctionhouse-throwaway

Then run:

npm run dev

If it reports missing dependencies:

npm install
npm run dev

Expected: Vite prints a local URL, usually:

http://localhost:5173

Open that URL in the browser.

Completion checkpoint

  • The homepage contains six sample auctions.

  • Selecting an auction opens its detail page.

  • All three themes can be selected.

  • The four course skills are installed.

Leave the practice server running and keep this same Codex chat. Tab 06 continues here.

tabs.name: 06 Browser Use & AGENTS.md
tabs.html:
Tab 06 — Browser Use and Project Instructions

Outcome: Ask Codex to verify the practice site in a browser and create useful project instructions.

Continue in the same auctionhouse-throwaway project and chat from Tab 05. Leave workshop unchanged.

1. Confirm the practice server is running

If it stopped, run in the practice project's terminal:

cd ~/codex-course/auctionhouse-throwaway
npm run dev

Expected: the server prints its URL. Use that URL in the next steps.

2. Ask Codex to demonstrate the site

Paste into the same Codex chat:

Use Playwright with a visible Chrome or Edge window to check
the practice auction site.

Verify:
1. The homepage displays six sample auctions.
2. Selecting an auction opens its detail page.
3. All three themes can be selected.

Use the running development server's URL.
Report what passed and any problems you find.

Expected: a browser window opens and Codex clicks through the site, then reports which of the three checks passed. If browser automation needs setup, let Codex explain the required installation. If it is unavailable in your environment, do those checks manually.

3. Create AGENTS.md

AGENTS.md stores instructions that Codex uses when working in this project.

Paste into Codex:

Create an AGENTS.md for this practice project.

Inspect the project first. Keep the instructions concise and include:
- The technology and conventions to preserve.
- The actual commands for installing, running, and checking the project.
- The browser checks required after relevant changes.

Do not invent commands or repeat information that is easy to
discover from the source files.

Expected: a new AGENTS.md file in the practice project.

4. Review and shorten the instructions

Open the generated file:

code ~/codex-course/auctionhouse-throwaway/AGENTS.md

Keep

Remove

Important constraints and conventions

Long descriptions of the current interface

Commands that actually exist

Invented test commands

Useful verification steps

Repeated or vague advice

Rules that help future work

Details likely to become outdated

Optional, only if you also use Claude Code: create a CLAUDE.md containing:

@AGENTS.md

Completion checkpoint

  • The homepage, detail route, and theme switching have been checked.

  • AGENTS.md exists and contains concise, accurate instructions.

  • You can explain why project instructions need maintenance.

tabs.name: 07 Run the Foundation
tabs.html:
Tab 07 — Run the Auction Application's Foundation

Outcome: Switch from the practice project to workshop and verify the frontend → API → database connection.

1. Close the practice project

In the terminal running the practice server, press:

Ctrl+C

Close its browser windows and remove the auctionhouse-throwaway project from Codex's project list.

Optional cleanup: move only ~/codex-course/auctionhouse-throwaway to Trash using Finder.

2. Read the workshop's instructions

Run in Terminal:

code ~/codex-course/workshop

Expected: VS Code opens the workshop. Open the root AGENTS.md and find these rules:

  • Use the prescribed technology stack.

  • Work in the designated part folder.

  • Record design decisions before implementation.

  • Build small, reviewable slices.

  • Run relevant checks and verify browser behavior.

3. Open the workshop in Codex

Add or select:

~/codex-course/workshop

Use Local work on the current branch. No worktree is needed for this lesson.

4. Install and start Part 1

Make sure Docker Desktop is running.

Run in Codex's terminal:

cd ~/codex-course/workshop/part-1-foundation
npm install
npm start

Expected: dependencies install, then the database setup and application servers start. Keep the terminal running.

Open the frontend:

http://localhost:5101

5. Verify the full connection

Open the health endpoint through the frontend:

http://localhost:5101/api/health

Expected: a successful response containing:

{
  "ok": true,
  "db": "ok"
}

Additional fields, such as a request identifier, may appear.

Completion checkpoint

  • The workshop is selected in Codex.

  • Part 1 opens at http://localhost:5101.

  • The health endpoint reports a successful database connection.

  • Parts 2–8 remain empty.

tabs.name: 08 Plan Mode & Grilling
tabs.html:
Tab 08 — Plan Mode and Grilling Before Building

Outcome: Define Part 2's behavior, review the plan, and let Codex begin the first slice.

Start a new chat inside workshop, using Local work and Medium reasoning. Docker should remain running.

1. Try Plan mode

Type into Codex:

/plan

Expected: Plan mode can be selected and its indicator appears. Turn it off before continuing.

Type /grill without sending it.

Expected: the installed grilling skills appear. Clear the text afterward.

2. Start Part 2's design conversation

Paste into Codex:

I want to add the ability to post auctions and make bids.
These should be stored in PostgreSQL using the database
service defined in docker-compose.yml.

GRILL ME WITH DOCS!

Work in part-2-create-auction-and-bid. Copy the foundation
from part-1-foundation and build on it there.

Follow the workshop rules: ask at most two rounds of questions,
document the decisions, and propose reviewable vertical slices.
Wait for approval before implementing.

Expected: Codex asks design questions (at most two rounds) and does not write feature code yet.

3. Answer the design questions

Match answers by topic, not question number. Codex's wording and option letters may differ.

Topic

Course decision

Users

Ten seeded demo users with a footer switcher; no real authentication

Listing fields

Title, category, description, condition, location, starting price, and closing time

Images

Category illustrations; no uploads

Publication

Auctions become visible immediately

Time

Future closing time stored as a UTC timestamp

Money

USD, stored as integer cents

Existing catalog

Seed the six existing auctions into PostgreSQL

Reset

An explicit reset restores Part 2's seed data; normal startup preserves changes

Active user

Initially remember the selection in localStorage; Tab 09 changes this

Seller

The active user becomes the seller; sellers cannot bid on their own auctions

Minimum bid

At least $1 above the current amount, enforced by the API

Ended auctions

Disable bidding in the UI and reject bids in the API

Bid history

Show bidder, amount, and time

Posting

A Sell link opens /auctions/new; successful posting opens the new detail page

Specifications

New listings do not require specifications; hide the section when empty

Concurrent bids

Handle sequential bidding now; defer concurrency protection to Part 3

If a question is unclear, reply:

Please explain that question with a simple example before I decide.

4. Review the documented plan

Ask Codex to show:

  • The agreed decisions in GRILL.md and any accompanying design documents.

  • A Mermaid diagram showing browser → API → PostgreSQL.

  • The proposed implementation slices and browser checkpoints.

Expected slices:

  1. Database-backed marketplace and user switching.

  2. Post an auction.

  3. Place bids and inspect bid history.

5. Approve only the first slice

Once the plan matches your decisions, send:

Approve the slices. Implement Slice 1 only, run the relevant
checks, verify it in the browser, and stop for my review
before starting Slice 2.

Open the workshop in VS Code if needed:

code ~/codex-course/workshop

Expected: part-2-create-auction-and-bid fills with the copied foundation and new implementation, and GRILL.md reflects the agreed rules.

Completion checkpoint

  • Design decisions are documented.

  • The diagram and slices match the intended application.

  • Codex has begun Slice 1 only.

  • Concurrency protection remains explicitly deferred to Part 3.

Continue in this same chat for Tab 09.

tabs.name: 09 Review Auctions & Users
tabs.html:
Tab 09 — Review Auctions and Users

Outcome: Review Part 2's first slice, verify it in the browser, and request a small follow-up change.

Continue in the same workshop chat from Tab 08. Don't approve Slice 2 yet.

1. Inspect the database and API

Open Codex's changed-files view. A diff shows added and removed lines.

In VS Code, open Part 2's migration under server/migrations/. Filenames may vary.

Item

What to verify

Users

Ten seeded demo users

Auctions

Six seeded listings, each linked to a seller

Bids

Fields for auction, bidder, amount, and timestamp

Money

Integer cents

Closing time

A timestamp representing the agreed closing instant

Then inspect the API routes and test names.

Expected read operations:

GET /api/users
GET /api/auctions
GET /api/auctions/:slug

Posting and bidding are later slices.

2. Check the decisions and verification evidence

Run in Terminal:

code ~/codex-course/workshop/part-2-create-auction-and-bid/GRILL.md

Expected: the file matches Tab 08's decisions.

Read Codex's completion summary. Look for actual results from:

  • Relevant automated tests.

  • TypeScript checks.

  • Browser verification.

3. Verify Slice 1 yourself

Run in Terminal (skip if Codex left the app running):

cd ~/codex-course/workshop/part-2-create-auction-and-bid
npm install
npm start

Open:

http://localhost:5102

Expected:

  1. The catalog displays the seeded auctions.

  2. The footer user switcher works.

  3. The selected user survives a reload under the initial design.

  4. Searching for memory finds the relevant listing.

  5. An auction detail page shows its seller and price.

Also open:

http://localhost:5102/api/users

Expected: the ten demo users as JSON.

4. Request the user-selection change

Paste into the same Codex chat:

Randomly assign an initial user for each new browser tab.
Keep that user's identity stable through navigation and reloads
within the tab, and retain the footer user switcher.

Show the active user's name at the top right instead of
"10 Demo users".

Update GRILL.md to reflect the changed decision and run the
relevant tests. Stop after this change; do not start Slice 2.

Expected: Codex changes the user selection, updates GRILL.md, runs the tests and stops without starting Slice 2.

Completion checkpoint

  • Slice 1 matches the agreed database and API design.

  • You have checked the catalog, search, details, and user switcher.

  • Codex has received the random-user follow-up.

  • Slice 2 has not started.

tabs.name: 10 Bidding & Concurrency Bug
tabs.html:
Tab 10 — Complete Bidding and Reproduce the Concurrency Bug

Outcome: Finish Part 2, verify ordinary bidding, then demonstrate why simultaneous bids need additional protection.

Stage 1 — Finish Part 2

Continue in the same Codex chat from Tab 09.

1. Verify the user-selection change

Open:

http://localhost:5102

Expected:

  • The active user's name appears at the top right.

  • A newly opened tab receives an initial random user.

  • Reloading preserves that tab's selected user.

  • The footer switcher still works.

Two tabs may randomly receive the same user; use the switcher when you need distinct identities.

Save the completed first slice:

cd ~/codex-course/workshop
git add -A
git commit -m "Part 2 slice 1: auctions and users"

2. Build Slice 2: posting auctions

Paste into the same Codex chat:

Slice 1 looks good. Continue with Slice 2: posting an auction,
following our agreed plan.

Run the relevant checks and verify the form in the browser.
Stop for review before starting Slice 3.

When Codex finishes, open Sell and post an auction:

Field

Example

Title

Classroom GPU

Category

GPUs

Description

Auction created during our workshop

Starting price

$100

Location

Your city

Closing time

At least 30 minutes ahead

Expected: the new listing opens, survives a refresh, and appears in catalog and search.

Commit:

git add -A
git commit -m "Part 2 slice 2: post auctions"

3. Build Slice 3: bidding

Paste into Codex:

Continue with Slice 3: bidding and bid history,
following our documented decisions.

Verify seller self-bidding rejection, minimum bid increments,
ended-auction rejection, and accepted bids.

Keep simultaneous-bid protection deferred to Part 3.

Run the relevant tests and browser checks, then stop for review.

Verify using the seller's tab and another tab with a different user:

Action

Expected behavior

Seller tries to bid

Bidding is unavailable; API also rejects it

Another user bids $100

Rejected: at least $1 above the starting/current amount is required

Another user bids $101

Accepted and shown in bid history

Another user bids below the new minimum

Rejected

Seller refreshes

Updated price and bid history appear

Bid on an ended auction

Rejected

Commit the finished Part 2:

git add -A
git commit -m "Part 2 slice 3: bidding rules"

4. Context management

If available, find Codex's context-usage indicator and Compact command. At a completed checkpoint, compaction summarizes the conversation history. For a new task, start a new chat.

Checkpoint: Posting and sequential bidding work. Part 2 is committed. Concurrency remains intentionally unprotected.

Stage 2 — The race condition

5. Find the vulnerable sequence

Open Part 2 in VS Code:

code ~/codex-course/workshop/part-2-create-auction-and-bid

Find the bid handler, typically in server/src/app.ts. Search for:

INSERT INTO bids

Expected: the handler follows this sequence:

Read current price → Validate bid → Insert bid

Two requests can both read the same old price before either inserts its bid. Sending one bid, waiting, then sending another does not expose this; the requests must overlap.

6. Start a new Codex chat

Keep workshop selected. Leave Part 2 running.

Paste into the new chat:

Inspect the bidding endpoint in part-2-create-auction-and-bid.

GRILL ME WITH DOCS.

Use at most two questioning rounds. Document our decisions
and propose two reviewable slices. Do not implement the

Answer the questions by topic, using these course decisions:

Topic

Decision

Concurrency

Serialize bidding using a transaction and an auction-row lock

Validation

Read the current price and validate after acquiring the lock

Stale bids

Reject amounts below the updated minimum; refresh the displayed state

Resubmission

No automatic bid resubmission

Clock

Inject an application clock so tests can control time

Acceptance time

Check time after acquiring the lock

Deadline

Reject bids at or after the closing instant

UI

Switch to "Ended" and disable bidding when the deadline arrives

Tests

Replace duplicate-reproduction assertions with protected-behavior assertions

Scope

Keep it simple; defer idempotency keys and extra retry mechanisms

Expected: GRILL.md, an architecture diagram, and two proposed slices:

  1. Serialized bidding and stale-bid recovery.

  2. Testable clock and closing-time behavior.

Stop for review before Slice 2.

→ Validate
→ Insert accepted bid
COMMIT

Make the frontend switch to Ended and disable bidding at the
deadline. Recheck the state when a backgrounded tab becomes active.

Run the relevant tests, type checks, and browser verification.

Useful for

Following one workflow across components

Agree on:
